Jory Pike.narrative: I fish the harbour from a boat that isn't mine, and I owe half the quay a little and pay most of it back when the catch is good. My mother has fed me on credit all my life, and now I'm courting Nia Wrack, and her mother looks at me like a bad tide. I'm cheerful about it, mostly. The debts will sort themselves out; a man with a good arm and a borrowed boat can always find work on the water.

memories.gist: The night the surge came, I was out on the harbour mouth and rowed back through the wreckage of the lower quay; I pulled a neighbour's boy out of the water and never found his father.
My mother's stall at the tide steps, the smell of frying fish and the way she'd slip a bowl to anyone who looked hungry, no marks asked.
The first time Nia Wrack laughed at one of my jokes and didn't stop, at Ilse Ostrander's noodle stall after the night crews came in.
Wick Gull's boat laid up, so I crewed for him a whole season and learned the deep water past the harbour mouth; I still owe him a share of one catch.
My mother took to her bed with the cough last winter and Mira Sallow's medicines pulled her through; I heard her tell Mira she'd pay when the season turned.

stances.why: A man who pays nothing gets no boat lent to him twice.
My mother fed half the quay on credit; that's how it's done, and it comes back round.
Nia won't go against Odile Wrack, and I wouldn't ask her to.
I've been behind before and the tide always brought something in.
My mother says it, and she's right; a wall doesn't fill a belly.

Jory Pike.calling: I'm a harbour fisherman — a borrowed boat now, but the water's mine as much as anyone's.

Sella Pike.narrative: I've kept a fried-fish stall by the tide steps for thirty years and fed half the quay on credit, and now the lean season has come round and I'm the one who owes. Mira Sallow's medicines kept me breathing through the winter and I haven't paid her a mark of it. My Jory is a good lad with a borrowed boat and a sweetheart, and I wish he'd ask the girl properly instead of leaving me to watch Odile Wrack's face. The stall-keepers are starting to talk about who pays and who doesn't, and I can hear my name in it.

memories.gist: The surge took the lower quay and the houses on it, and I fried fish all night for the families who came up the steps with nothing but what they stood in.
The winter the cough took me, Mira Sallow came with her medicines three times and wouldn't take a mark; I told her I'd pay when the season turned.
Jory's father drowned before the surge, and I raised the boy on the stall, teaching him to gut a fish before he could read.
The lean season when the boats came in light and I kept feeding the crews on credit, telling myself the quay pays its debts.
The first time Jory brought Nia Wrack to the stall and she ate two bowls and laughed at his jokes, and I saw he was lost.

stances.why: A hungry neighbour is a debt you pay with a bowl, not a tally.
I've fed half the quay on credit; I won't be the one who turns the talk ugly.
A wall doesn't fill a belly; the Warden should feed the terrace first.
Jory needs someone to count the marks with him, and Nia Wrack is that someone.
I'll pay Mira Sallow before the stall-keepers can say I didn't.

Sella Pike.secret: I've been selling the stall's best fish cheap to Lyss Fenner under the counter so I can put by a few marks for Mira without anyone seeing me save.

Sella Pike.calling: Thirty years I've fried fish by the tide steps, and I'd have it no other way — a hot meal for anyone who comes down hungry.
